text: Thomas Crapper's name is on every toilet joke you've ever heard,

fields.title: Thomas Crapper Didn't Invent the Toilet
fields.subtitle: Knossos, Harington, Cumming, and the name that stuck

visual: Episode title card as the famous name is introduced.

text: and a lot of people will tell you, with a straight face, that he invented the toilet
visual: Slow push-in on the Crapper portrait as the popular claim is stated.

source.rights: Public domain: author anonymous, 19th century, published before 1 January 1931, as stated on the file page
source.credit: Portrait of Thomas Crapper, unknown photographer (source: MJC Plumbing), via Wikimedia Commons

text: and that's why we call it what we call it.

fields.headline: Many people say he gave the toilet its name
fields.sub: The popular claim, not the history

visual: Text card: the claim, attributed to 'a lot of people'.

text: But a man in England built a flushing toilet for Queen Elizabeth I nearly three centuries before Crapper's patents,
visual: Elizabeth I portrait, slow push-in, as the queen is named.

source.rights: Public domain photographic reproduction, as described in the search result; re-read the file page tag before use
source.credit: Darnley Portrait of Elizabeth I, National Portrait Gallery, London, via Wikimedia Commons

notes: The man is not named in this beat; the portrait is of the queen only.

text: and the word "crap" is older than Crapper is.

fields.headline: The word "crap" is older than Crapper

visual: Text card.

text: Now, to be fair, Thomas Crapper was a real person who really did make toilets better,
visual: Crapper portrait again, slow push-out.

source.rights: Public domain: author anonymous, 19th century, published before 1 January 1931, as stated on the file page
source.credit: Portrait of Thomas Crapper, unknown photographer (source: MJC Plumbing), via Wikimedia Commons

text: and we'll give him his due, but he wasn't first, not even close.

fields.headline: Crapper wasn't first, not even close
fields.sub: Full credit for what he really did

visual: Text card; sub lands on 'his due'.

text: The famous version goes like this, a man named Thomas Crapper invents the flush toilet,

fields.title: The famous version

steps.label: Thomas Crapper invents the flush toilet
His name becomes the slang
steps.sub: He puts his name on it

fields.caption: The story as it is usually told

visual: Two-box flow, first box lit: the famous version.

text: puts his name on it, and his name becomes the slang.

fields.title: The famous version

steps.label: Thomas Crapper invents the flush toilet
His name becomes the slang
steps.sub: He puts his name on it

fields.caption: The story as it is usually told

visual: Same flow, second box added.

text: It's a perfect story, because the name does all the work, right?

fields.label: Thomas Crapper
fields.crop: Tight crop on the face, slow push-in (closer than 01-b and 01-f)

visual: Crapper portrait, tight push-in.

source.rights: Public domain: author anonymous, 19th century, published before 1 January 1931, as stated on the file page
source.credit: Portrait of Thomas Crapper, unknown photographer (source: MJC Plumbing), via Wikimedia Commons

text: You hear Crapper and toilet in the same sentence and your brain just files it as true.

fields.headline: Crapper plus toilet: the brain files it as true

visual: Text card.

text: And a lot of that comes from one book. In 1969 a writer named Wallace Reyburn
visual: Flow build, step 1: 1969, Wallace Reyburn.

text: published a book called Flushed with Pride, and it's partly tongue-in-cheek,
visual: Flow build, step 2: the book title and its hedge.

text: it's partly a joke, and it helped spread the idea that Crapper invented the toilet.
visual: Flow build, step 3: the idea spreads.

text: So a book that was partly kidding ended up being where a lot of people's facts came from.
visual: Flow build, step 4: people's facts came from it.
notes: No book cover shown: the 1969 cover is a copyrighted toilet illustration.

text: So who did it first? Well, it depends how far back you want to go,

fields.headline: Who did it first? It depends how far back

visual: Text card.

text: so let's start way back. The palace at Knossos, on the island of Crete,

fields.title: Knossos, Crete
fields.caption: The palace at Knossos, on the island of Crete

visual: Schematic map with one pin: Knossos, Crete.
notes: Knossos is at about 35.298 N, 25.163 E. 'first' is false so no FIRST tag.

text: had latrines that were flushed with water and drained into stone sewers,
visual: Modern photo of the Knossos ruins, slow push-in.

source.rights: CC BY-SA 4.0, as stated in the search result (photographer Theofanis Ampatzidis, 17 August 2017)
source.credit: Theofanis Ampatzidis, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

notes: Modern photo of the site, not of the latrines. Some Knossos photos include early-20th-century restorations; the label says only 'modern photograph'.

text: and that's about 3,500 years ago, somewhere around 1700 to 1450 BC.

fields.caption: Water-flushed latrines at Knossos, about 3,500 years ago

visual: Date stamp with the hedged range.

text: Now, I want to be careful here, because you'll hear people say
visual: Second Knossos photo, slow pan, as the careful caveat begins.

source.rights: CC BY-SA 3.0 Unported, as stated in the search result (uploader Lemur12)
source.credit: Lemur12, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

text: the Minoans had a flush toilet with roof cisterns, and that's overstated.

fields.headline: The Minoan flush-toilet claim is overstated
fields.sub: Careful: this is not a modern toilet

visual: Text card. The headline carries the hedge; the phrase from the narration is deliberately not shown on screen.
notes: The narration here contains the myth's wording. Keep that wording off screen: the card names the claim only as 'the Minoan flush-toilet claim'.

text: It didn't have a cistern and a valve like a toilet in your house,
visual: Compare card: a modern toilet versus Knossos.

text: the water came from rainwater channelled from the roof,
visual: Flow build, step 1: rainwater from the roof, through the drains.

text: and through the drains, or somebody poured water in,
visual: Flow build, step 2: or somebody poured water in.

text: and either way it flushed the waste into a sewer.
visual: Flow build, step 3: waste into a sewer.

text: So it's not a modern toilet, but it's water carrying waste away, about 3,500 years ago.

fields.headline: Not a modern toilet: water carrying waste away

visual: Text card.

text: And Knossos wasn't even the earliest. Homes in the Indus Valley had drained latrines even earlier,

fields.title: Drained latrines, even earlier
fields.caption: The Indus Valley: drained latrines even earlier than Knossos

visual: Schematic map: Knossos and the Indus Valley.
notes: Mohenjo-daro is at about 27.329 N, 68.139 E and stands in for the Indus Valley. No Indus date is shown: the notes leave the c. 2600 BCE date out.

text: and one review says almost every house there had its own bathroom, including a lavatory.

fields.label: Mohenjo-daro, an Indus Valley city (modern photograph)
fields.lower: Mohenjo-daro, an Indus Valley city (modern photograph)

visual: Modern photo of a street at Mohenjo-daro, slow push-in.

source.rights: Not stated in the search result (photographer Saqib Qayyum, 8 March 2014); read the file page license

notes: Illustrates the place only, not the review's claim. If rights are unusable, fall back to a text card: 'One review: almost every house had a bathroom'.

text: So the idea of a toilet that carries waste away with water
visual: Third Knossos photo, slow push-in.

source.rights: CC BY-SA 2.0 Generic, as stated in the search result
source.credit: cavorite (Flickr), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0

text: is a lot older than Thomas Crapper, it's thousands of years older.
visual: Datecard: Knossos versus Crapper, gap in the script's words.

text: But if you want the thing we'd actually recognise, a bowl fed by a tank of water,
visual: Flow build, step 1: a bowl fed by a tank of water.

text: the name you want is Sir John Harington. In 1596, Harington built a flushing toilet with a cistern
visual: Harington portrait, slow push-in on the name.

text: for Queen Elizabeth I, and a cistern is just the tank,
visual: Elizabeth I portrait, slow push-out.

source.rights: Public domain photographic reproduction, as described in the search result; re-read the file page tag before use
source.credit: Darnley Portrait of Elizabeth I, National Portrait Gallery, London, via Wikimedia Commons

text: the water sits up there and when you let it go
visual: Flow build, step 2: you let the water go.

text: it flushes the bowl. So that's a cistern-fed bowl, a working model,
visual: Flow build, step 3: it flushes the bowl.

text: built for the Queen of England, in 1596.

fields.caption: Harington builds a flushing toilet with a cistern for Queen Elizabeth I

visual: Date stamp: 1596.

fields.sub: Of the flush toilet with a tank

text: And there's more, because a toilet that flushes isn't the whole job.

fields.headline: A flushing toilet isn't the whole job

visual: Text card.

text: If you've got a pipe running straight from your bathroom down to a sewer,
visual: Flow build, steps 1 to 3: bathroom, pipe down, sewer.

text: you've also got a pipe running straight from the sewer back up into your bathroom,
visual: Flow build, step 4: the pipe back up.

text: and everything that smells comes right back up it.
visual: Flow build, step 5: the smell comes back up.

text: The fix for that is the S-bend, a bend in the pipe
visual: Flow build, step 1: the S-bend, a bend in the pipe.

text: that holds a little water in it all the time,
visual: Flow build, step 2: it holds a little water.

text: and that water blocks the smell from coming back up.
visual: Flow build, step 3: the water blocks the smell.

text: And the S-bend was patented in 1775 by a man named Alexander Cumming.
visual: Cumming portrait with the date lower-third.
